title: Stonehenge
summary: Stonehenge, on Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire, England, is a Neolithic and Bronze Age monument. A circular ditch and bank were dug about 3000 BCE, the sarsen and bluestone settings were raised from about 2500 BCE, and the stones were rearranged over the following centuries. UNESCO calls it the most architecturally sophisticated prehistoric stone circle in the world.

uncertainty.note: Start is the digging of the circular ditch and banks, 'about 3000 BC' (English Heritage); astronomical year -2999. The stones were set up 'in about 2500 BC' and the Y and Z holes are radiocarbon dated to 1800-1500 BC. UNESCO places the whole complex's 2000 years of use between circa 3700 and 1600 BC. End is the present: the monument stands as a ruin.

phases.description: Circular ditch with inner and outer banks, about 100 m across with two entrances, dug about 3000 BC; the stones follow.
Stones set up in the centre in about 2500 BC; sarsens near the entrance and the four Station Stones raised at about the same time.
About 200 or 300 years later the central bluestones were rearranged into a circle and inner oval, later altered to a horseshoe; the Avenue built.
The Y and Z holes were dug, radiocarbon dated to 1800-1500 BC; they may mark a rearrangement never completed.
Only six lintels of the outer sarsen circle remain in place. The sources opened do not date the collapse or removal of stones; this phase starts where recorded construction ends.

materials.material: sarsen sandstone for the outer circle, lintels and horseshoe trilithons, sourced from an area about 15 miles north of the site
'bluestones' (up to 80, brought from the Preseli Hills in south-west Wales)

reviewer_note: Shape ring: the outer sarsen circle (30 m across) and its concentric settings. Least sure of the height: English Heritage gives sarsens 'up to 7 metres tall' (the central horseshoe trilithons) and the outer circle's lintel underside at 4 m, but no figure for the top of the outer lintels, so the 7 m height is the tallest stones, not the ring. The start of the ruined phase is not sourced; only the end of recorded construction is. Coordinates are UNESCO's first listed point for property 373 (the other lies at Avebury).
